replacement: If the reader has rightly understood what I have already said about literature in general, he will have no difficulty seeing what kind of influence a democratic social condition and democratic institutions can have on language itself, which is the chief instrument of thought.

problem: 'language must naturally partake' softened to 'naturally shares' (force of 'must' lost).
replacement: In aristocracies, language must naturally share in the state of repose in which everything else stays. Few new words are coined, because few new things are made; and even if new things were made, they would be called by familiar words whose meaning has been fixed by tradition. If the human mind does at last stir itself, or is roused by light breaking in from outside, the new expressions it introduces carry a degree of learning, intelligence, and philosophy that shows they do not originate in a democracy. After the fall of Constantinople turned the tide of science and literature toward the west, the French language was almost immediately flooded with a multitude of new words, all with Greek or Latin roots. A learned neologism then sprang up in France. It stayed within the educated classes and had no noticeable effect on the people, or at most a very gradual one. All the nations of Europe showed the same change in turn. Milton alone introduced more than six hundred words into the English language, almost all of them derived from Latin, Greek, or Hebrew. In a democratic community, by contrast, the constant agitation tends unceasingly to change the character of the language, just as it changes the look of public affairs. In the midst of this general stir and rivalry of minds, a great number of new ideas are formed. Old ideas are lost, or reappear, or are subdivided into an infinite variety of minor shades. The result is that many words must fall out of use, and others must be brought in.

problem: Causal connective 'for' dropped; the second clause gives the reason for borrowing.
replacement: Lacking knowledge of the dead languages, democratic nations are inclined to borrow words from living tongues, for their dealings with one another become constant, and the inhabitants of different countries imitate each other more readily as they grow more alike every day.

problem: 'I know not whether this loose style has not some secret charm' (a suspicion that it has) rendered as the neutral 'I do not know whether ... has some secret charm', dropping the second negation and changing the hedge.
replacement: These abstract terms, which abound in democratic languages and are used on every occasion without being attached to any particular fact, enlarge and obscure the thoughts they are meant to convey. They make the mode of speech more concise and the idea in it less clear. But where language is concerned, democratic nations prefer obscurity to labor. In fact, I wonder whether this loose style does not have some secret charm for those who speak and write among these nations. The men who live there are frequently left to the efforts of their own individual minds, so they are almost always prey to doubt. And since their situation in life is forever changing, they are never held fast to any of their opinions by the secure tenure of their fortunes. People living in democratic countries are therefore inclined to have unsettled ideas, and they need loose expressions to convey them. They never know whether the idea they express today will suit the new position they may occupy tomorrow, so they naturally develop a liking for abstract terms. An abstract term is like a box with a false bottom: you may put in it whatever ideas you please, and take them out again without being noticed.

problem: 'the wildest range' changed to 'the widest range' (different word, loses the sense of unbounded freedom).
replacement: I am convinced that in the end democracy turns the imagination away from everything external to man and fixes it on man alone. Democratic nations may amuse themselves for a while by considering the productions of nature, but they are truly excited only by a survey of themselves. Here, and here alone, are the true sources of poetry among such nations to be found. It may be believed that poets who neglect to draw their inspiration from this source will lose all sway over the minds they want to enchant, and will be left in the end with none but unmoved spectators of their raptures. I have shown how the ideas of progress and of the indefinite perfectibility of the human race belong to democratic ages. Democratic nations care little for what has been, but they are haunted by visions of what will be. In this direction their unbounded imagination grows and expands beyond all measure. Here, then, is the wildest range open to the genius of poets, which lets them place their works at a sufficient distance from the eye. Democracy shuts the past against the poet, but opens the future before him. All the citizens who make up a democratic community are nearly equal and alike, so the poet cannot dwell on any one of them. But the nation itself invites the exercise of his powers. The general similarity of individuals makes any one of them, taken separately, an improper subject of poetry. Yet it allows poets to include them all in the same imagery and to take a general survey of the people itself. Democratic nations have a clearer perception than any others of their own aspect, and an aspect so imposing is admirably suited to the portrayal of the ideal.

problem: Source's 'for as the multitude seeks ... it has neither the time' (reason for the hopes not being disappointed) restructured with an added 'therefore' that changes the logical link.
replacement: The authors, for their part, do not fail to obey a tendency they share themselves. They perpetually inflate their imaginations and expand them beyond all bounds, and they not infrequently abandon the great in order to reach the gigantic. By these means they hope to attract the attention of the multitude and to fix it easily upon themselves. Nor are their hopes disappointed, for as the multitude looks for nothing in poetry but subjects of very vast dimensions, it has neither the time to measure accurately the proportions of all the subjects set before it, nor a taste correct enough to perceive at once in what respect they are out of proportion. The author and the public corrupt one another at the same time.
